summary: Renames the three-bit EXP field in the MPLS label stack entry to Traffic Class, since it is now used as a class of service marker rather than being experimental. It updates many earlier RFCs for consistent naming. This is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A box on a shipping label was called experimental, but everyone used it to mark how urgent a parcel is. This renames the box to match what it does.

questions: what is the mpls traffic class field
why was the mpls exp field renamed
subtitle: The MPLS label field once called EXP gets a name that matches what it does: Traffic Class.

tldr.problem: The 3-bit EXP field in the MPLS label stack entry was labeled 'reserved for experimental use', so other standards bodies and implementors assumed they could use it for other purposes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC renames the field to Traffic Class (TC) everywhere it occurs, rewrites the affected text in RFC 3032, RFC 3270 and RFC 5129, and says all other references to EXP now mean TC.
tldr.outcome: The wire format is unchanged. Only the name and the stated purpose change, and the RFC updates 13 earlier RFCs for consistency.

today: RFC 5462 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It updates RFC 3032, 3270, 3272, 3443, 3469, 3564, 3985, 4182, 4364, 4379, 4448, 4761 and 5129, for example RFC 3032 and RFC 3270.

sections.title: Why the Field Was Renamed
sections.content:
RFC 3032 defines the MPLS label stack entry with a three-bit field called EXP, described only as reserved for experimental use. From the start it was meant to carry Class of Service information, and early drafts of RFC 3032 even called it the Class of Service field. The use was not agreed in time, so it was marked experimental and the name stuck.

That designation led other standards bodies and implementors to assume the field could serve other purposes. The authors rejected the plain name 'CoS field' because later work widened its use: RFC 3270 defined E-LSPs, which use it to pick the Diffserv behavior, and RFC 5129 added explicit congestion marking. The chosen name, Traffic Class (TC), relates to an MPLS packet the way the IPv6 TC field relates to an IPv6 packet.
sections.plainLanguage: A box on a form said 'for tests only', but everybody used it to say how important the package was. So it got a new name that says what it is for.

sections.title: Text Changed in Earlier RFCs
sections.content:
In RFC 3032 the section titled 'Experimental Use' becomes 'Traffic Class (TC) field'. The new text says the three-bit field carries traffic class information, and that the rename applies to all places it occurs in IETF RFCs and other IETF documents. Figure 1 of RFC 3032 changes Exp to TC.

RFC 3270 gets a note that every reference to the EXP field now means the TC field, and a new terminology entry for TC. The acronym E-LSP is kept because it is in widespread use, but now stands for 'Explicitly TC-encoded-PSC LSP'. RFC 5129 gets the same note, and its bullet on per-domain ECT checking is reworded to say TC.

Other RFCs are covered by one rule: references to the 'Exp field', 'Exp bits', 'EXP bits' or 'EXP' now mean the TC field. The RFC names RFC 3272, 3443, 3469, 3564, 3985, 4182, 4364, 4379, 4448 and 4761 as examples.
sections.plainLanguage: The new name is written into the old rule books, and a note says that anywhere the old name shows up, read it as the new one.

sections.title: The Scope of the Rename
sections.content:
Several RFCs that the document updates explicitly refer to the field in different ways: 'Exp field', 'Exp bits', 'EXP bits' or just 'EXP'. In every one of those places the reference now means the TC field. This holds for all RFCs, including but not limited to the ones the RFC lists.

For the RFCs other than RFC 3032, RFC 3270 and RFC 5129, the update is limited to the name of the label stack entry field. RFC 3270 and RFC 5129 already described how the field is used, but did not explicitly state that they update RFC 3032. This document records that fact.
sections.plainLanguage: Wherever an old book says the old name, you just read the new name. Nothing else in those books changes.

sections.title: How the TC Field Is Used
sections.content:
The field has only a few bits, so using it for QoS and ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification) functions is meant to be flexible, and those functions may rewrite all or some of the bits.

Current implementations look at the TC field with and without label context. It may be copied to label stack entries that are pushed onto the stack, so that new entries do not have different TC values from the rest of the entries.
sections.plainLanguage: The little urgency mark can be changed along the way, and new labels stuck on the pile usually copy the same mark.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that it only changes the name of one field in the MPLS shim header, and so introduces no new security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: Only a name changed, nothing new works differently, so nothing new can go wrong.
